# StockSaathi

> StockSaathi (also written Stock Saathi) is a free stock market simulator and paper trading app for students and beginners in India, including Indian teens aged 13 to 18. Users practise investing with ₹1,00,000 of virtual money on real NSE and BSE stocks, ETFs and mutual funds at real market prices, and an AI coach flags beginner mistakes, such as panic-selling and FOMO buying, as they make them. It is built for complete beginners, uses no real money, and is not a broker or investment adviser.

StockSaathi teaches by doing rather than through lessons: there are no course modules or quizzes. Learning comes from placing practice trades, being coached on your own decisions, replaying real Indian market crashes, and reviewing a report card that grades decision quality.

## Key facts

- Price: free. No paid plan, no subscription, no in-app purchases; it never asks for payment details.
- Audience: Indian teens aged 13–18, school and college students, and complete beginners. Built for students and open to anyone in India learning to invest; anyone 13 or older can sign up.
- Money: ₹1,00,000 of virtual money per account. Nothing can be deposited, withdrawn or converted into anything real. No real shares are bought or sold.
- Markets: 4,000+ stocks listed on the NSE and BSE (including NSE SME listings), 300+ ETFs and 8,000+ active mutual fund schemes, at real market prices. Prices can be delayed; it is not a live trading feed. No futures and options, crypto or foreign stocks.
- Orders: market orders, limit orders and after-market orders (AMOs). Pending orders are filled on the server even when the app is closed.
- AI coach ("Saathi"): checks every trade for nine common mistakes — panic-selling, FOMO buying, pump-chasing, anchoring to 52-week highs or lows, single-stock concentration, sector concentration, the disposition effect, churning and overtrading — and explains what it noticed in the user's own numbers. It answers finance questions in English, or in Hinglish when Hinglish mode is switched on in Settings. It never recommends buying or selling a security and does not predict prices.
- After-trade notes: when a trade fits one of the nine patterns, a short note appears after the order goes through, explaining it in the user's own numbers (for panic-selling: the fall, the stock's usual daily move and the result). It never blocks or delays an order. Every indexed stock page also lists that stock's real falls since 2011 or its listing: how often they recovered, how long that took, and which never did.
- Crash replays ("Time Travel"): day-by-day replays of the COVID-19 crash (2020), the 2008 global financial crisis and the 2016 demonetisation shock, built from real daily Nifty 50 closes, comparing a ₹1,00,000 portfolio that held with one that sold everything on day three and stayed in cash. Results: in the COVID-19 replay (19 Feb to 9 Nov 2020) holding finished 5.6% ahead; in the 2008 replay (8 Jan to 27 Oct 2008) selling early won, because the Nifty fell 60%; in the demonetisation replay (8 Nov 2016 to 28 Feb 2017) holding finished 7.0% ahead. Featured AI-built replays cover the Harshad Mehta scam (1992), the dot-com crash (2000), Satyam (2009), IL&FS (2018), DHFL (2019), YES Bank (2020), the Paytm IPO (2021) and the Adani–Hindenburg report (2023); users can generate replays of other events.
- Report card: a letter grade from A+ to D that updates after every decision and weighs behaviour more than returns, with badges for habits like diversifying and holding long term.
- What it is not: StockSaathi at stocksaathi.co.in never sells subscriptions, stock tips, trading signals or trading bots. Unrelated products use similar names.
- Real investing for under-18s: in India a minor cannot open a trading account independently; a guardian can open and operate a demat account in the minor's name. StockSaathi needs no demat account, broker or money.
- No leaderboard: there is deliberately no leaderboard ranking users by returns.
- News: Indian market headlines from major business news sources, tagged bullish, bearish or neutral.
- Without an account, visitors can browse markets and charts, read news, chat with the AI coach and play the curated crash replays. Trading and keeping a portfolio need a free account.
- Founder: Founded and built by Ali Arbab, a student developer from India; launched 19 April 2026. Profile: https://stocksaathi.co.in/about · LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/thealiarbab
- Contact: Support: grievance@stocksaathi.co.in · Business, partnerships and press: business@stocksaathi.co.in
- Compliance: StockSaathi is an educational simulator. It is not a SEBI-registered broker, investment adviser or research analyst, and is not affiliated with SEBI, NSE or BSE. Any account and its data can be deleted on request via grievance@stocksaathi.co.in.

## Guides

- [The 2008 crash in India: why selling early won, and why that's rare](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/2008-crash-india): In 2008 the Nifty 50 fell 59.9% in ten months, so selling early won; it took until November 2010 to get back, and no fall since has been as deep.
- [52-week highs, lows and the anchoring trap](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/52-week-high-anchoring): A 52-week high is a stock's highest price of the last year; on 30 October 2026 half the Nifty 50 was 20% or more below it, and anchoring on that number is a common trap.
- [Diversification for beginners: why putting most of your money in one stock is risky](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/concentration-risk): Of 423 large and mid-sized Indian stocks, 53.2% were 30% or more below their high in late 2026, against 12.4% for the Nifty 50, which is why one stock is riskier than a basket.
- [What happened to ₹1 lakh in the Nifty 50 during the COVID crash (2020)](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/covid-crash-2020-nifty): ₹1,00,000 in the Nifty 50 fell 37.2% in 33 days in 2020; holding ended at ₹1,02,764 by 9 Nov 2020, selling on day three at ₹97,295.
- [Can a teenager open a demat account in India?](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/demat-account-minor-india): A minor can hold a demat account run by a guardian, but SEBI says a minor can't contract with a broker to buy or sell; trading accounts are sell-only.
- [Demonetisation and the stock market: what happened from November 2016 to February 2017](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/demonetisation-stock-market): After demonetisation on 8 November 2016 the Nifty 50 fell 7.4% to its low on 26 December 2016 and was back above its starting level by 25 January 2017.
- [Large-cap stocks that recovered fastest from falls since 2011](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/fastest-recovering-large-caps): Across 86 Nifty 100 companies with at least five recovered 10% falls since 2011, the typical median recovery was 67.5 trading days, from 25 for the fastest to 318 for the slowest.
- [FOMO in the stock market: what it is, and what happened after big run-ups](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/fomo-investing): After 463 sharp run-ups in large Indian stocks since 2011, the typical next 60 sessions were not worse than normal, but outcomes spread far wider in both directions.
- [Market order, limit order and AMO explained, with examples](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/market-limit-amo-orders): A market order fills now at the best available price, a limit order only at your price or better, and an AMO is placed while the market is closed and runs at the next open.
- [Mutual funds, stocks and ETFs explained for beginners](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/mutual-funds-stocks-etfs-explained): A stock is a share of one company, a mutual fund pools money and issues units at the day's NAV, and an ETF is a basket that trades on an exchange like a share.
- [How long does the Nifty 50 take to recover from a 10%, 20% or 30% fall?](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/nifty-recovery-time): Every 10%+ fall in the Nifty 50 since its November 2010 high with its recovery time: the median was 200 trading days; the only 30% fall was COVID-19 in 2020.
- [Nifty 50 and Sensex: what they are and how they're calculated](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/nifty-sensex-explained): The Nifty 50 tracks 50 large NSE companies and the Sensex 30 on the BSE, both weighted by free-float market value; the Nifty rose 265.8% from November 2010 to October 2026.
- [NSE and BSE explained: what is the difference?](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/nse-and-bse-explained): NSE and BSE are India's two main stock exchanges; many companies list on both, so one share can show two slightly different prices at the same moment.
- [Panic selling: what it is, why beginners do it, and how to stop](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/panic-selling): Panic selling is selling out of fear during a fast fall; StockSaathi's coach flags it after the trade, and 99.7% of sales on StockSaathi since 25 Oct 2026 didn't fit the pattern.
- [What is the P/E ratio? Explained with real Indian stocks](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/pe-ratio-explained): The P/E ratio is a share's price divided by its earnings per share; on 6 November 2026 eight large Indian companies ranged from 10.47 to 49.99.
- [Share market kaise sikhe: bina paise ka 4 hafte ka practice plan](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/share-market-kaise-sikhe): A Hinglish four-week plan to learn the share market with virtual money: key words, first practice trades, a crash replay and reviewing your own mistakes.
- [What is a SIP? Explained with a real Nifty 50 backtest](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/sip-explained-nifty-backtest): ₹5,000 a month in the Nifty 50 from January 2015 to October 2026 put in ₹7,10,000 and reached ₹12,66,619, a yearly return of 9.4% before costs and dividends.
- [T+1 settlement in India explained, with worked examples](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/t-plus-1-settlement): Indian stock trades settle one working day after the trade (T+1), for all stocks since 27 January 2023; optional same-day T+0 began on 28 March 2024.
- [What Indian students buy first when they start investing](https://stocksaathi.co.in/learn/what-students-buy-first): On StockSaathi, Reliance Industries is the most common first buy (25.1% of first trades) and 67.9% of first buys are Nifty 50 companies.
